# Introduction {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## Outline {.smaller}

1. **The problem** — A model whose target variable is changing
2. **NACE 2.1 and the multivocal codes** — Why a simple mapping is not enough
3. **Human and virtual annotation** — Combining expert and machine knowledge
4. **Methodology** — A constrained, context-augmented LLM pipeline
5. **Infrastructure** — Open-source MLOps on the SSPCloud
6. **Results** — Performance of the retrained classifier
7. **An alternative: pure RAG** — When no legacy labels exist
8. **Conclusion and perspectives**

::: {.notes}
Here is the roadmap for the next twenty minutes. I will start by framing the problem — what specifically breaks when an official classification is revised. Then I will describe NACE Rev. 2.1 and the central technical difficulty: what we call "multivocal" codes, where one old code maps to several new ones. I will explain how we combined a human annotation campaign with a virtual one based on Large Language Models. I will then walk you through the methodology, the infrastructure we built on top of open-source tools, and the empirical results. I will close with a discussion of an alternative approach based on retrieval-augmented generation, which we are currently exploring for situations where no legacy labels exist at all.
:::

# 1. The Problem {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## Machine learning models in official statistics

- More and more ML models are being **deployed in production** at Insee
- Multiple use cases for **automatic coding**:
  - **NACE** (economic activity)
  - **COICOP** (household consumption)
  - **ISCO / PCS** (occupations)
  - **CPA** (products)
- **Today's focus**: the principal economic activity of enterprises (APE — based on NACE)

::: {.callout-note}
## Quality Assurance Framework of the European Statistical System
> Source data, integrated data, intermediate results and statistical outputs must be **regularly assessed and validated**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Like many of your institutes, Insee has been moving an increasing number of machine learning models into production. We have several active classification use cases — household consumption coded against COICOP, occupations against ISCO, products against CPA — but the one I will focus on today is the coding of the principal economic activity of enterprises, which we call APE in France and which is based directly on the European NACE classification.

A point worth stressing here: under the European Statistical System Quality Assurance Framework, statistical outputs must be regularly assessed and validated. This applies to ML models as well — they are not "set and forget". They need maintenance, and that maintenance becomes especially demanding when the target variable itself changes.
:::

## The data source: a regulatory shift

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
**The PACTE Law (January 2023)**

- All business filings now go through a **single online portal**
- Operated by the **INPI**
- Replaces the historical network of CFE (Business Formality Centres)
- **Free-text** activity descriptions, no longer normalised
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Example of an incoming description**

> *"I want to develop my activity in the cleaning and maintenance of office buildings: emptying bins, vacuuming, mopping the floor"*

➡️ Noisy, colloquial, often misspelled
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
A bit of context on the data we deal with. Since January 2023, following the PACTE Law in France, every business formality must be filed through a single online portal operated by the National Institute for Industrial Property — the INPI. This replaced a historical network of intermediaries, the Business Formality Centres or CFE, where human agents would help structure and clean the activity descriptions.

The consequence of this reform is that we now receive raw, unstructured, free-text descriptions written directly by the entrepreneur. As you can see in the example, they are colloquial, sometimes ungrammatical, often misspelled. The volume is high — several thousand new businesses every day — so manual coding is not feasible at scale. This is precisely why automatic classification is essential for us.
:::

## SIRENE and the historical model

- **SIRENE** = the French business register since the 1970s
- Allocates the **SIREN**, **SIRET**, and **APE** identifiers
- Recently migrated to **SIRENE 4**: real-time, streaming architecture
- The legacy expert system **SICORE** could only auto-code about **30 %** of cases
- **End of 2022**: deployment of a supervised ML model (fastText)
  - ➡️ Now auto-codes around **65 %** of incoming filings
  - The remainder is sent for manual review

::: {.notes}
SIRENE is the French business register, and it has been operating since the 1970s. It assigns three identifiers: the SIREN — the legal entity number — the SIRET for each establishment, and the APE code, which is the principal economic activity. You see the APE printed on every receipt in France.

Last year SIRENE migrated from a batch architecture to a real-time streaming one — this is what we call SIRENE 4. With this volume and the diversity of free-text inputs, the old expert-rule system, SICORE, could only handle around 30 percent of cases automatically. So at the end of 2022 we deployed a supervised ML model based on fastText, which now auto-codes about 65 percent of the incoming flow, with the rest going to human review.

This is the production setting. Now imagine that the target classification of this model is about to change.
:::

## What breaks when a classification is revised?

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Standard ML maintenance**

- Inputs may drift over time
- We monitor and **retrain on fresh labels**
- The target variable stays the **same**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Classification revision**

- The **target variable itself changes**
- New labelled data are **scarce or missing**
- Legacy labels are in the **wrong space**
- Standard retraining is **not possible**
:::

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Central question**: how can we leverage years of accumulated production knowledge in the old classification to bootstrap a model in the new one?
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the structural problem at the heart of my talk. In normal machine learning maintenance, what changes over time is the input distribution — what we call data drift — and you address it by retraining on fresh manually labelled data. The target variable, the Y you are predicting, stays the same.

When a classification is revised, the situation is fundamentally different. The Y itself changes. The codes you trained on no longer exist, or their semantic content has shifted. Newly labelled data in the new nomenclature are either unavailable or, at best, very limited — because human annotation in a brand-new classification is slow, expensive, and requires experts who are themselves still learning the new rules.

So the central question of our project becomes: we have ten million labels in the old classification reflecting years of production knowledge — how can we leverage this asset to bootstrap a model in the new one, without waiting two or three years for a fresh manually-labelled corpus?
:::

# 2. NACE 2.1 and the Multivocal Codes {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## NACE Rev. 2.1: the timeline

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **2025** — Dual coding period
  - SIRUS: full historical recoding by end of 2025
  - SIRENE: integration of NACE 2.1 in flow + MLOps infrastructure
- **2026** — Quality improvement of the new coding
- **2027** — NACE 2.1 becomes the production standard, NACE 2.0 maintained in parallel
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Scope of the change**

- Level 5 (sub-classes): **746** vs **732** previously
- Mostly splits at level 4 (class)
- But also some merges and recompositions
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Let me give you the timeline. NACE Rev. 2.1 is being adopted progressively across European statistical institutes. At Insee, 2025 is a dual-coding year: our structural business register, SIRUS, is being fully recoded by the end of the year, while SIRENE — the live business register — is integrating the new classification in flow, together with a new MLOps infrastructure. The year 2026 is dedicated to quality improvement, and in 2027 NACE 2.1 becomes the production standard, while we continue to maintain the old coding in parallel for continuity.

In terms of magnitude, the change is significant but not revolutionary. At the most detailed level — level 5, which we call sub-classes — we go from 732 categories to 746. Most of the changes are splits at the class level, but there are also a few merges and recompositions. The headline number, 746 versus 732, hides the real complexity, which I will now describe.
:::

## Univocal vs. multivocal mappings

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Univocal codes** (1-to-1)

- 551 classes
- Direct mapping
- Trivially recoded
- ✅ The easy case
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Multivocal codes** (1-to-N)

- 181 classes
- One source code → several target codes
- Up to **38** candidates in extreme cases
- ⚠️ Requires expert judgement on the activity description
:::

:::

**The problem cannot be solved by a deterministic mapping table alone.**

::: {.notes}
Here is the central technical difficulty. The correspondence between NACE 2.0 and NACE 2.1 is not a bijection. We have two kinds of cases.

The univocal codes are easy: 551 classes have a one-to-one mapping. You apply the correspondence table and you are done. No ambiguity, no decision to make.

The multivocal codes are the hard part. We have 181 classes where one old code maps to multiple possible new codes — sometimes two, sometimes three, but in some extreme cases up to 38 candidate target codes for a single source code. In those cases, the correspondence table alone cannot tell you which new code is right. You need to look back at the actual activity description of the enterprise and apply expert judgement to disambiguate. And that, fundamentally, is a classification task in itself.
:::

## How big is the multivocal problem in practice?

**Training set**: ~2.7 million observations from SIRENE 4

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### In the correspondence table
| Multivocal | Univocal |
|------------|----------|
| **25 %**   | 75 %     |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### In our actual training set
| Multivocal | Univocal |
|------------|----------|
| **52 %**   | 48 %     |
:::

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
➡️ **~1.4 million observations** that cannot be recoded by a table lookup
:::

::: {.notes}
We were initially hopeful that, even though some codes are multivocal in theory, they would be rare in practice. Unfortunately, this hope was misplaced.

If you look at the correspondence table itself, the proportion is reasonable — about 25 percent of theoretical codes are multivocal. But once you weight by the actual distribution of observations in our training set, that figure jumps to 52 percent. More than half of the data points we need to recode fall into the ambiguous cases.

In absolute numbers, this means roughly 1.4 million observations from SIRENE 4 that cannot be automatically recoded by a simple table lookup. That is far too many for human experts to process in any reasonable timeframe. So we needed another solution.
:::

# 3. Human and Virtual Annotation {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## Two annotation campaigns

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1. Gold standard in NACE 2.0
- ~10,000 annotations in the **current** classification
- 6 expert annotators from the **SIRENE Quality Office**
- Blind annotation, no auto-coding aid
- Purpose: **validate** the precision of the legacy labels
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 2. Ground truth in NACE 2.1
- ~30,000 annotations on **multivocal cases**
- ~25 APE business experts across France
- Candidate codes pre-filtered using the NACE 2.0 code
- Purpose: **benchmark** for our LLM pipeline
:::

:::

For each item, an annotator can: **assign a code**, **delegate** to a peer, or mark as **uncodable**.

::: {.notes}
We launched two annotation campaigns. The first one was an audit of the existing system. We had ten thousand observations annotated blind in the current NACE 2.0 classification by six experts from the SIRENE Quality Office, with no auto-coding aid. The purpose was not to train a model but to verify that our legacy labels — the labels we will rely on as input to our LLM pipeline — were of sufficient quality. This is the gold standard.

The second campaign is the one that matters most for what follows. We mobilised our entire network of about twenty-five APE business experts across France to annotate roughly thirty thousand observations directly in NACE 2.1. We focused on multivocal cases because that is where the difficulty is. To save time, the candidate codes were pre-filtered using the NACE 2.0 code already known. This produces our ground truth — the reference dataset against which we evaluate everything else.

In both campaigns, annotators have three possible actions: assign a code, delegate the task to another annotator if they feel they lack expertise, or mark the description as uncodable if it is too vague. Interestingly, in both campaigns we observed roughly 6 percent of delegations and 6 percent of uncodable cases — a stable signal that we found valuable for calibrating expectations.
:::

## Reconciling expertise and innovation

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- 30,000 annotations are **valuable but insufficient** for a high-performing classifier
- Manual annotation **does not scale** to 1.4 million observations
- LLMs can process volume, but **lack the domain context**
- ➡️ Combine the two: **virtual annotators guided by expert knowledge**
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Hybrid principle**

::: {style="text-align:center;"}
🧑‍🏫 Expert<br>↓<br>📚 Codified knowledge<br>↓<br>🤖 LLM as virtual annotator<br>↓<br>📊 Volume + Quality
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
So we have two complementary resources. On one side, thirty thousand high-quality manual annotations in the new classification — too few to train a high-performing classifier from scratch, but very valuable as a benchmark. On the other side, the ten million labels accumulated over years of production in the old classification — a massive asset, but expressed in the wrong target space.

The intuition we built on is the following. Human experts have something that no language model has natively: a deep, context-specific understanding of how the classification rules apply to noisy real-world descriptions. But experts cannot scale to a million observations. Language models can scale, but they need that expertise injected as context in order to make sound decisions.

So the idea was to use language models as virtual annotators — to reproduce the expert workflow at scale, with the human expertise crystallised into structured prompts and reference materials.
:::

# 4. Methodology {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## Recasting the task as constrained selection

- The full label space (746 NACE 2.1 codes) is too large and unstable
- For each observation, we already know the **NACE 2.0 code**
- The correspondence table tells us the **set of admissible NACE 2.1 codes**
- ➡️ The task becomes: **pick the right code from a short, restricted list**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Key benefit**: this dramatically reduces the search space and aligns the model with official classification guidelines.
:::

::: {.notes}
The first methodological choice was to reframe the task. Instead of asking the language model to classify the activity description into one of 746 possible NACE 2.1 codes — which is hard, error-prone, and offers many opportunities for hallucination — we exploit a piece of information we already have: the existing NACE 2.0 code, which has been validated through years of production.

For each observation, we use the correspondence table to retrieve the set of admissible NACE 2.1 codes — typically two to five candidates, occasionally more. The language model is then asked to pick the right one from this short list. This is a constrained selection problem rather than an open classification problem. The search space drops from hundreds to a handful, the prompt is more manageable, and we stay aligned with the official classification rules.
:::

## The pipeline

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
**For each observation**:

1. Retrieve the activity description (free text)
2. Retrieve the legacy NACE 2.0 code
3. Use the correspondence table to get the set of candidate NACE 2.1 codes
4. Inject the **explanatory notes** of each candidate code into the prompt
5. Ask the LLM to pick the most appropriate code
6. Parse the structured JSON response

This is a form of **Context-Augmented Generation (CAG)** with a manual retriever.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
**Inputs to the prompt**

| Element | Source |
|---------|--------|
| Activity text | SIRENE 4 |
| NACE 2.0 code | Production model |
| Candidate set | Correspondence table |
| Explanatory notes | Official NACE 2.1 documentation |
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Here is the pipeline in more detail. For each observation, we assemble a prompt that contains four pieces of information: the free-text activity description as written by the entrepreneur, the legacy NACE 2.0 code from production, the list of candidate NACE 2.1 codes from the correspondence table, and — this is crucial — the explanatory notes from the official NACE 2.1 documentation for each candidate code.

This last element is what brings real expert knowledge into the prompt. Explanatory notes are the official prose definitions written by the classification authority, often containing inclusion and exclusion rules that allow you to disambiguate between two close candidates. By injecting them into the prompt, we give the language model the same reference material that a human expert would consult.

We can describe this technically as a form of context-augmented generation. It is similar to retrieval-augmented generation, but the retriever is not a vector search — it is a deterministic lookup based on the legacy code and the official correspondence table. We will see later that we are also experimenting with a fully RAG-based variant.
:::

## The prompt structure

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
**System prompt** — same for every observation

> *You are an expert in the NACE classification. Your task is to assign a NACE 2.1 code to a business based on its activity description, using a candidate list derived from the existing NACE 2.0 code…*

**User prompt** — observation-specific
- Activity description
- Legacy NACE 2.0 code
- Candidate codes + explanatory notes
- Required output schema
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Expected output**

```json
{
  "codable": true,
  "nace_2008_valid": true,
  "nace2025": "0147J"
}
```

- `codable`: was the description sufficient?
- `nace_2008_valid`: is the legacy code consistent with the description?
- `nace2025`: the chosen code (or `null`)
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The prompt itself has two parts. There is a system prompt — identical for every observation — that defines the role of the model as a NACE classification expert and gives the general instructions: analyse the description, pick the most appropriate code from the provided list, return null if you are not confident, and respond strictly in JSON.

Then there is a user prompt that is specific to each observation, containing the activity description, the legacy code, the candidate set with explanatory notes, and the required output schema.

The output is a structured JSON with three fields. The codable field tells us whether the description was sufficient at all. The nace_2008_valid field is a useful side benefit: the model also flags when it suspects the legacy code itself was incorrect — which can happen and which is information we would not have obtained otherwise. And the nace2025 field is the actual recoding decision.

Forcing the model into structured JSON output is essential for production. Language models tend to be verbose and chatty by default. Without an explicit format constraint, you get free-text answers that are very expensive to parse reliably and lead to errors at scale.
:::

## Why context matters: an illustration

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Without context** (system prompt only)

- The model returns a code, but in the **old** NACE 2.0
- It "knows" the old classification from training data
- It does **not** know NACE 2.1 — too recent
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**With context** (candidate set + notes)

- The model retrieves the right code in **NACE 2.1**
- The output respects the JSON schema
- The decision is **traceable** to the explanatory notes
:::

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Without context, the model hallucinates. With context, it disambiguates.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Let me illustrate why context is so essential here. We tested the same activity description on a public model with just the system prompt — no candidate set, no explanatory notes. The model produces a code, but it produces a NACE 2.0 code. Why? Because NACE 2.0 has been around for fifteen years; it is in the training data of every commercial language model. NACE 2.1 was published only recently and is barely represented in any pre-training corpus. So without the explicit context, the model falls back on what it knows.

When we add the candidate set and the explanatory notes, the model retrieves the correct NACE 2.1 code, respects the output format, and — importantly — the decision is traceable. We can see exactly which information the model had access to when making its choice. This is essential for an official statistical institute, where every methodological decision must be auditable.
:::

## Multi-model annotation

| Model | Size | Inference speed | Performance | Behaviour |
|-------|------|-----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Qwen 2.5 | 32B | Slow | Strong | Very restrictive |
| Ministral | 8B | Very fast | Reasonable | Permissive |
| Mistral Small | 24B | Slow | Strong | Moderately restrictive |
| Llama 3.1 | 70B (quantised) | Very slow | Very strong | Moderately restrictive |

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Aggregation strategies**: cascade · majority vote · weighted vote
:::

::: {.notes}
We did not rely on a single model. We queried four open-source language models in parallel — Qwen 2.5, Ministral, Mistral Small, and a quantised Llama 3.1 70B. They differ along several axes: size, inference speed, raw performance, and what we call restrictiveness — that is, how often they decline to answer when uncertain. Some are very cautious, some are quite permissive.

Treating each model as an independent virtual annotator, we tested several aggregation strategies. A cascade approach where we trust one model first and fall back to others. A simple majority vote. A weighted vote where each model's contribution is weighted by its individual accuracy on the ground truth set.

The intuition behind aggregation is the same as in any ensemble method: complementary errors cancel out. A weak permissive model and a cautious strong model can together produce a more robust labelling than either alone. In our experiments, majority voting served as a strong baseline.
:::

# 5. Infrastructure {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## A fully open-source MLOps stack on the SSPCloud

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **SSPCloud**: Insee's cloud-based data science platform
- Entirely **open-source** stack
- Reproducible, auditable, scalable
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

| Component | Tool |
|-----------|------|
| LLM serving | **vLLM** |
| Prompt management | **Langfuse** |
| Experiment tracking | **MLflow** |
| Workflow orchestration | **Argo Workflows** |
| Containers | **Kubernetes** |

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
A few words about the infrastructure. We are big believers in open-source, and the entire pipeline runs on what we call the SSPCloud — Insee's internal data science platform, which is itself open-source and based on Kubernetes.

For language model serving, we use vLLM, which is the de facto standard for high-throughput inference on open-source models. For prompt management, we use Langfuse — every prompt is versioned, every model run is traceable to a specific prompt version. For experiment tracking, MLflow — we log all hyperparameters, all evaluation metrics, the full lineage of every model. For orchestration, Argo Workflows, so the entire pipeline is reproducible end-to-end as a containerised workflow.

This stack is not exotic — many of you may already be using parts of it. The point I want to make is that for an official statistical institute, this kind of traceability is not optional. Every label produced by an LLM in our training set must be reproducible: we must be able to point to the exact prompt version, the exact model version, and the exact correspondence table version that produced it. Without that, we could not justify using LLM-generated labels in a production statistical pipeline.
:::

# 6. Results {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## Evaluation: how do you grade an LLM annotator?

- **Reference**: the ~30,000 manually annotated multivocal cases
- Three complementary metrics:
  1. **Overall accuracy** — across all observations
  2. **Accuracy on codable cases** — when the description is sufficient
  3. **LLM-only accuracy** — errors imputable to generation alone

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Insight**: a substantial share of disagreements are not LLM errors but ambiguous descriptions or even legacy-coding mistakes.
:::

::: {.notes}
Evaluation is genuinely difficult here, and I want to be honest about it. Our reference is the thirty thousand manually annotated cases, which themselves contain some level of human disagreement and error.

We use three complementary metrics. Overall accuracy is the headline figure: how often does the LLM agree with the human ground truth on all observations. Accuracy on codable cases restricts to observations where the description was deemed sufficient by the experts — this isolates the genuine classification difficulty from the noise of unusable descriptions. And what we call LLM-only accuracy attempts to factor out errors that are not really errors of the model: cases where the description is genuinely ambiguous, or where the legacy NACE 2.0 code was itself wrong.

This third metric is methodologically important because it tells us when the LLM is doing well at the task we actually asked it to do, as opposed to inheriting upstream noise. A naive evaluation can underestimate the model substantially.
:::

## Reconstructing the training set

- ~1.4 million multivocal observations relabelled via the LLM pipeline
- Combined with the **1.3 million univocal** observations (table lookup)
- ➡️ **~2 million observations** in NACE 2.1
- Distribution across codes is **very close** to the original SIRENE 4 distribution

::: {.callout-tip}
This is what we call **semi-synthetic data**: labels are generated algorithmically, but grounded in real observations and structured domain knowledge.
:::

::: {.notes}
Once we are satisfied with LLM performance on the benchmark, we apply the pipeline at scale. The 1.3 million univocal observations are recoded by simple table lookup — no model needed. The 1.4 million multivocal observations go through the LLM pipeline. We discard observations where no model was sufficiently confident. The result is a reconstructed training corpus of about two million observations in NACE 2.1.

A point worth highlighting: the distribution of codes in this reconstructed corpus is very close to the original SIRENE 4 distribution. We do not introduce a major bias by going through the LLM. This is reassuring because it means the downstream classifier will see a representative sample of the actual flow of incoming filings.

I prefer the term semi-synthetic for this kind of data. It is not pure synthetic data — every observation corresponds to a real business with a real activity description. But the labels are produced algorithmically rather than by humans. The grounding in real observations and in structured official documentation is what makes us comfortable using these labels for production training.
:::

## Performance of the retrained classifier

- A **fastText**-style classifier (and a more recent transformer-based model) is trained on the reconstructed corpus
- Standard ML practice: **train / validation / test** split, data editing, monitoring
- ➡️ Overall accuracy of approximately **80 %** — comparable to the previous-generation NACE 2.0 model

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Take-away**: semi-synthetic LLM-generated labels can substitute for manual annotations in the early stages of a classification transition.
:::

::: {.notes}
The decisive question, of course, is whether a classifier trained on these LLM-generated labels can match the performance of one trained on real human labels. We trained two variants — a fastText-style model in line with our current production system, and a more recent transformer-based architecture using a library called TorchTextClassifiers, developed in-house and presented separately by my colleague Meilame Tayebjee.

Following standard ML practice — train, validation, test splits, data editing on the reconstructed corpus, monitoring of distribution shifts — we obtain an overall accuracy of about 80 percent, which is comparable to what the previous-generation NACE 2.0 model achieves on its own task.

The take-away here is, I think, the most important point of the talk. Semi-synthetic labels generated by language models can effectively substitute for manually annotated data in the early stages of a classification transition. This was not obvious at the start of the project. The fact that we recover the same level of accuracy as a model trained on years of production-curated labels is a strong empirical signal that the approach is operationally viable.
:::

# 7. An Alternative: Pure RAG {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## When no legacy labels exist

The CAG pipeline assumes:

- a **legacy classification** with reliable labels
- an **official correspondence table** to the new classification

What if neither is available?

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- A **completely new classification** without predecessor
- Use cases in **another country / institute** without an existing model
- A different domain altogether (e.g., COICOP for households)
:::

::: {.notes}
The CAG approach I just described relies on two assumptions: that you have reliable legacy labels in an old classification, and that there is an official correspondence table to the new one. For NACE 2.1, both are available. But this is not always the case.

You may be facing a brand-new classification with no predecessor. You may be at an institute that does not yet have a production model in the old classification. You may be applying this approach to a completely different domain — for instance, COICOP coding of household consumption — where there is no equivalent legacy infrastructure. In all these cases, the legacy code is not there to constrain the candidate list, and the CAG approach does not directly apply.
:::

## Retrieval-Augmented Generation

- Build a **vector database** of the explanatory notes of the new classification
- For each observation:
  1. Embed the activity description
  2. Retrieve the **top-k most similar** NACE 2.1 codes
  3. Inject these candidates and their notes into the prompt
  4. Let the LLM pick

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Benefits**

- No reliance on legacy labels (which may themselves contain errors)
- More flexible: works when no historical labels exist
- Natively handles **new** activities without precedent
:::

::: {.notes}
The alternative we are exploring is fully retrieval-augmented generation. The idea is to skip the legacy code entirely and rely directly on a vector database containing the descriptive notes of the new classification.

Concretely, for each observation, we embed the activity description, retrieve the top-k most similar NACE 2.1 explanatory notes from the vector store, inject those candidates into the prompt, and let the LLM pick the most appropriate one.

This approach has two important benefits. First, it does not depend on legacy labels, which themselves can contain human annotator errors that we would otherwise propagate. Second, it is much more flexible: it works in any setting where you have an authoritative classification with explanatory notes, even if you have no historical model. It also handles genuinely new activities — emerging sectors that did not exist in the old classification — more gracefully than a correspondence-table approach.
:::

## A parallel use case: COICOP

- Automatic coding of consumption items in a **household survey**
- Smaller volumes than SIRENE
- Suitable testbed for the RAG approach
- Promising results, but **higher inference cost** than CAG
- ➡️ Trade-off: flexibility vs. computational cost

::: {.notes}
We have been testing this RAG approach in parallel on a different use case: the automatic coding of consumption items in a household survey, against the COICOP classification. The volumes there are much smaller than SIRENE — a few hundred thousand items at most — which makes it a comfortable testbed for an approach that is computationally heavier than CAG.

Early results are encouraging, and we expect this to become a complementary tool in our portfolio. But there is a real trade-off: pure RAG requires embedding inference and vector search at every observation, which is significantly more expensive at scale than the CAG pipeline that relies on a deterministic correspondence table. For SIRENE, with its millions of observations and real-time flow, CAG remains the preferred approach for now. For surveys and one-off recoding tasks, RAG is very attractive.
:::

# 8. Conclusion and Perspectives {.section-title background-color="#1e3a8a"}

## What we have shown

::: {.incremental}
- A **practical methodology** to handle classification revisions in production ML
- LLMs as **virtual annotators** can scale where humans cannot
- Constrained selection + context-augmented generation = **traceable, auditable** decisions
- Semi-synthetic labels reach **production-grade accuracy** (~80 %)
- Fully open-source, reproducible MLOps stack
:::

::: {.notes}
To summarise. We have shown that classification revisions, which are a structural challenge in production ML for official statistics, can be addressed pragmatically using large language models. The key methodological idea is to treat language models as virtual annotators — and to constrain them tightly using the correspondence table and the official explanatory notes, so that their decisions remain traceable and auditable.

The empirical result is that a classifier trained on the reconstructed semi-synthetic dataset reaches accuracy levels comparable to the previous-generation production model. This is sufficient evidence, in our view, to proceed with operational deployment.

Equally important is the choice of stack: everything we did is open-source, runs on Kubernetes, and is fully reproducible. We are not locked into any vendor, and the methodology can be transferred to any institute willing to invest in similar infrastructure.
:::

## Limits and ongoing work

- **Cost of inference** — even with open-source models, two million queries is non-trivial
- **Drift in LLMs themselves** — model versions evolve quickly
- **Quality of the legacy labels** — we inherit upstream errors
- **Improving the RAG variant** — better embeddings, rerankers, hierarchy-aware retrieval
- **Extending to other classifications** — COICOP, ISCO, CPA…

::: {.notes}
A few honest words on limits. Inference at scale is not free, even with open-source models. Two million queries across multiple models requires careful workflow management and infrastructure budget. The language model ecosystem itself drifts: every six months there is a new generation, and reproducibility requires us to pin specific versions carefully. We also inherit the errors of the legacy labels — the LLM cannot fix what was wrong upstream, although in some cases it does flag suspicious legacy codes.

On the methodological side, we are working on improving the RAG variant: better embeddings tailored to the classification domain, rerankers to refine the retrieved candidates, and exploiting the hierarchical structure of NACE — section, division, group, class, sub-class — to do tree-style retrieval rather than flat similarity search. And we are extending the approach to other classifications: COICOP for consumption, ISCO and PCS for occupations, CPA for products.
:::

## Why this matters for official statistics

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Classification revisions are **inevitable** and **recurring**
- Traditional bottleneck: **wait for human annotations** before retraining
- LLM-assisted recoding **shortens this delay** dramatically
- ➡️ Better **continuity** of statistical outputs across revisions
- ➡️ Lower **operational cost** of nomenclature transitions
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**The broader question**

How can we use generative AI **responsibly** in official statistics?

- Reproducibility ✅
- Traceability ✅
- Open source ✅
- Human oversight ✅
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Stepping back to the bigger picture: classification revisions are a recurring fact of life in official statistics. NACE has been revised every fifteen to twenty years, and we have analogous cycles for COICOP, ISCO, and CPA. The traditional bottleneck has been the time required to accumulate enough human-annotated data in the new classification before any ML system can be retrained — typically two to three years of operational delay.

What this work shows is that LLMs can substantially shorten that delay, while preserving continuity of statistical outputs and lowering the operational cost of the transition. Beyond our specific case, I see this as part of a broader question that all of us in this room are facing: how do we use generative AI responsibly in official statistics? Our answer is that it is feasible, provided we maintain reproducibility, traceability, open-source tooling, and human oversight at every step.
:::
